title: A Record Cyclospora Outbreak With an Elusive Source
hook: A Cyclospora outbreak has now topped 4,100 cases — a U.S. record — even after the FDA retracted its lone positive lab test, leaving Taylor Farms lettuce as the prime suspect on epidemiology alone.
key_points: Cyclosporiasis, an intestinal illness causing diarrhea and nausea, surged across the U.S. in July 2026, reaching 31 states within days.
The FDA links the outbreak to lettuce distributed by Taylor Farms — but after retracting its only positive lab test as a false positive, the link now rests on epidemiology.
That lettuce was served at Taco Bell locations in Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, West Virginia, and Indiana.
By late July the CDC's tally topped 4,100 cases — more than double the mid-July count and a U.S. record for cyclosporiasis.
Officials warn the exact source may be hard to pin down definitively, putting the onus on consumers to be careful.
Cyclospora spreads through contaminated food or water, so handwashing and washing produce remain standard precautions.
content_html: Cyclosporiasis — an intestinal illness caused by the parasite Cyclospora that brings on diarrhea and nausea — is spreading fast across the U.S. As of July 10, the CDC's surveillance showed cases in 17 states, with Michigan alone reporting more than 1,250 cases. Just two days later, NPR reported the outbreak had grown to 31 states — more than half the country.
extra_html:
The CDC has opened a traceback investigation, but as of this reporting, the source of the contamination hasn't been identified. Past cyclospora outbreaks in the U.S. have often been traced to fresh produce, which is part of why food-safety experts point back to the basics when a source is still unknown: wash your hands, and wash your produce. Neither guarantees safety on its own, but they're the practical precautions available while investigators work out where this outbreak started. If you develop watery diarrhea that lasts more than a few days, it's worth checking in with a clinician.

As of July 15, the CDC had confirmed more than 1,600 cases nationwide, with over 140 people hospitalized — the outbreak's growth hadn't slowed, and the source was still unknown.

The investigation then pointed to a suspect. The CDC and FDA focused on shredded iceberg lettuce distributed by Taylor Farms and served at Taco Bell locations in Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, West Virginia, and Indiana. By July 17, the national case count had climbed to 1,644, making this one of the largest cyclosporiasis outbreaks on record.

But the source proved harder to nail down than it first looked. On July 20, the FDA retracted its single positive test for cyclospora on Taylor Farms lettuce, calling it a "false positive." The agency still believes the brand's lettuce is linked — but on epidemiological grounds now, not a confirmed lab hit, and it has cautioned that the exact source may be difficult to trace definitively. That uncertainty is exactly why the practical advice reverts to the basics that were there all along: while officials sort out the supply chain, the onus is on consumers to wash their hands and their produce, and to see a clinician for watery diarrhea that drags on more than a few days.

And the case count kept climbing. By July 23, NPR reported the CDC's tally for the year had passed 4,100 — more than double the mid-July count, and surpassing previous U.S. records for the parasite. Because confirming even a single case can take weeks, that figure likely lags the true spread, and it may keep rising as backlogged tests are counted. On July 24 the CDC reported the outbreak had expanded into four more states, and by late July the caseload — "4,100 and counting," per NPR — spanned at least nine Midwest states plus New York and North Carolina.

Attention then turned to why the source took so long to find. Speaking to NPR, NBC News health reporter Erika Edwards pointed at two federal changes. The CDC's FoodNet surveillance program — a partnership with 10 state health departments — scaled back last summer from tracking eight pathogens to just two, E. coli and salmonella, dropping Cyclospora, Listeria, and Shigella. Edwards was careful to say that cut "probably had very little impact on what we're seeing now," since FoodNet monitors trends rather than stopping outbreaks. The more consequential item, she said, is the Food Traceability Rule — which would require companies to keep careful records of where food is grown, where it goes, and how it gets there. It was due in January 2026 and has been pushed to July 2028. Food-safety experts told her that had it been in force, the source of this outbreak could have been identified a lot sooner.

flashcards.prompt: How fast is the 2026 cyclosporiasis outbreak growing?
flashcards.back_html: Fast — reported cases went from 17 states on July 10 to 31 states by July 12, with Michigan alone logging more than 1,250 cases.

flashcards.prompt: What did the FDA point to as the likely source of this cyclospora outbreak?

choices.text: Shredded lettuce distributed by Taylor Farms, served at Taco Bell in five states

flashcards.explanation_html: The FDA linked the outbreak to Taylor Farms lettuce served at Taco Bell in five states — though after retracting its one positive lab test as a false positive, the link now rests on epidemiology rather than a confirmed sample.

flashcards.prompt: Which five states does the FDA warn to avoid Taco Bell shredded lettuce in?
flashcards.back_html: Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, West Virginia, and Indiana — the states where the implicated lettuce supply was served, while the investigation continues.

flashcards.prompt: How large had the outbreak grown by late July 2026?
flashcards.back_html: More than 4,100 cases — more than double the mid-July count and a U.S. record for cyclosporiasis, even though confirming a single case can take weeks and Taylor Farms lettuce remains the leading suspect on epidemiology alone.
